content: The search identified two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), specifically in Kenya and South Africa, which exclusively included women living with HIV (WLHIV). These trials compared cryotherapy to large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) as treatment modalities for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) (Greene 2019 and Smith 2017). Additionally, two retrospective studies from a colposcopy clinic in the United Kingdom, involving women without HIV, compared thermal ablation to LLETZ (Papoutsis 2017 and 2018). The sample sizes in these studies ranged from 80 to 233 women per treatment arm. The lesions treated were CIN 2 and CIN 3, with no cases of carcinoma in situ (CIS) or adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). Follow-up durations varied between 6 and 24 months. Only one new study, Greene 2019, provided data stratified by CIN type. The findings were inconsistent with current knowledge regarding the comparative effects of ablative versus excisional treatments for CIN. Specifically, the recurrence rate was higher with LEEP (loop electrosurgical excision procedure) compared to cryotherapy in women with CIN 2, whereas the difference was less pronounced in women with CIN 3. A recent systematic review compared cold-knife conization (CKC) to LEEP in women with AIS. The included studies met the eligibility criteria, with the search date extending up to December 2015. The review, conducted by Jiang et al. (2017), highlighted the differences in outcomes between these two procedures, including the risk of positive surgical margins and residual disease rates. The WHO conducted a global, anonymous, cross-sectional online survey to assess the acceptability and preferences of women, including WLHIV, regarding cervical cancer screening and treatment. The survey targeted women aged 15 years and older and aimed to address gaps in knowledge identified in the literature. A total of 561 individuals responded, with 60% completing all questions. Respondents represented 68 countries, with the highest participation from the WHO AFRO region, particularly Ghana and South Africa. Among WLHIV, 25 individuals participated, with 17 reporting being on antiretroviral therapy. Responses were distributed across various age groups, with the best representation from women aged 35–39 and 55–59 years. The survey revealed that 94% of respondents had received a college or university education, indicating potential selection bias due to the online nature of the survey. Most respondents reported having undergone cervical cancer screening at least once, with higher rates observed in countries such as Nigeria, Kenya, India, the United Kingdom, the United States, Ghana, and South Africa. However, WLHIV reported lower screening rates compared to the general population. Notably, 42% of WLHIV indicated they were likely to face challenges in attending screening programs, compared to 17% of the general population. Common barriers included work-related issues, fear of pain, and a perception of low risk for cervical cancer. A strong preference for immediate treatment following a diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial lesions was observed, with 82% of the general population and 75% of WLHIV agreeing or strongly agreeing. Those who preferred delayed treatment often cited the need for adequate counseling, options, and time to decide. Written feedback highlighted discomfort with the use of a speculum during screening, with some respondents suggesting less intrusive diagnostic methods and better communication about potential side effects. The survey also explored the role of confidants in health-related decision-making. Spouses or partners were the most frequently cited confidants, followed by close friends or siblings. Among WLHIV, over 70% identified their spouse or partner as playing a critical role in their health decisions. The survey had several limitations, including selection bias due to its online nature, lack of validation of the survey instrument, and the use of a convenience sample, which may not be representative of specific populations or regions. Despite these limitations, the survey provided valuable insights into the acceptability and preferences of women regarding cervical cancer screening and treatment, particularly in the context of WLHIV. The findings underscore the importance of addressing barriers to screening and ensuring that treatment options are accessible and acceptable to all women.
